agency: DC Department of Human Services (DHS), Economic Security Administration (ESA)
admin_note: The District of Columbia is not a state but administers SNAP as its own single, unified jurisdiction — structurally like a state-administered program, not county-administered, with no sub-jurisdictional policy variation. DHS's Economic Security Administration (ESA) runs it centrally through ESA Service Centers District-wide. FLAGSHIP FINDING (correction of a widely-repeated false secondary-source claim, confirmed by TWO independent primary sources): several secondary sources (snapscreener.com, and multiple SNAP-eligibility-calculator content-farm sites) describe DC as having an ongoing districtwide ABAWD work-requirement waiver with 'work requirements not enforced anywhere in the District.' This pack fetched DHS's own live, actively-maintained SNAP Work Requirements page directly and found the opposite: DC's ABAWD work-requirement implementation STARTED June 1, 2026, with a fixed 36-month clock running June 1, 2026 - May 31, 2029 — DC's long-standing districtwide waiver was NOT renewed for FY2026. This pack independently cross-checked this against USDA FNS's own official ABAWD Time Limit Waivers FY2025-2029 index, which lists three FY2025 DC waiver-response entries (the most recent dated 05/21/2025) and NO FY2026 entry — corroborating, from a wholly separate federal source, that DC's waiver lapsed and was not renewed. SECOND FLAGSHIP FINDING (correction of a second false secondary-source claim, confirmed by TWO independent primary sources): several secondary sources (including one otherwise-detailed page) state that DC operates a SNAP Restaurant Meals Program (RMP) for elderly/disabled/homeless clients. This pack fetched USDA FNS's own official 'States that Operate a Restaurant Meals Program' list directly and DC is NOT on it (the list is: Arizona, Maryland, New York, California, Massachusetts, Rhode Island, Illinois (Cook/Franklin counties only), Michigan, Virginia) — and independently cross-checked DHS's own live SNAP consumer page, which lists 'Hot foods' and 'Prepared Foods fit for immediate consumption' as items you CANNOT buy with SNAP in DC, with no RMP exception mentioned. This pack's reading: DC does NOT operate an RMP, and the secondary-source claims to the contrary appear to conflate DC with its RMP-operating neighbors Maryland and Virginia. THIRD FINDING (structural, confirmed): DC runs the same TANF-funded-service categorical-eligibility (BBCE) mechanism family as this roster's Delaware and New Hampshire packs — DC Code § 4-261.02 grants categorical eligibility to all applicants at or below 200% FPL gross income via a Mayor-established TANF-funded program/service, codified directly in DC's own statute (DC Code Title 4, Chapter 2B, the 'Food Stamp Expansion Act'), not merely a generic USDA BBCE option description. FOURTH FINDING (confirmation of a minority-position claim, reached via direct statutory text rather than accepting a secondary-source label): several secondary sources correctly state DC has 'fully opted out' of the federal drug-felony SNAP ban, but this pack chased the underlying citation and confirms it directly: DC Code § 4-205.71 states plainly that 'an adult who is a drug felon shall not be denied cash or food assistance benefits...solely because he or she is a drug felon' — a full, unconditional opt-out enacted in 1999 and amended as recently as 2019, not a 'modified' ban of the kind many other states use. FIFTH FINDING (structural gap, disclosed not hidden): unlike Delaware's single consolidated DSSM 9000 manual, this pack found DC's SNAP-specific policy is NOT consolidated in one DCMR (DC Municipal Regulations) title/chapter — Title 29 DCMR ('Public Welfare') contains no chapter specifically titled for food stamps/SNAP eligibility rules the way DE's DSSM 9000 or many other states' manuals do; DC's state-specific SNAP policy instead lives primarily in DC Code Title 4, Chapter 2B (a codified STATUTE, not an agency-issued manual) plus DHS's own live, actively-maintained consumer pages. This pack also found and explicitly avoided a legacy-manual-mirror trap: dcrules.elaws.us's Title 29 DCMR mirror carries a page metadata tag reading 'D.C. Municipal Regulations (Last Updated: September 13, 2017)' — a nearly nine-year-stale unofficial mirror with no HTTP error signal — and did not rely on it for any current figure, using it only to confirm DCMR chapter-numbering structure. Confirm current operative practice with DHS ESA directly, the same caution this roster already carries for its other built jurisdictions.
system: DHS's Economic Security Administration (ESA) processes SNAP centrally District-wide (no sub-jurisdictional policy variation); applicants apply online through District Direct (districtdirect.dc.gov/ua/), in person at any ESA Service Center (e.g. 661 H Street NE, 1649 Good Hope Rd SE), by phone via the Public Benefits Call Center (202-727-5355), or by fax/mail. DC's standard certification period is 12 months; the Elderly Simplified Application Project (ESAP) assigns a 36-month certification period to households where all members are elderly (60+) and/or disabled with no earned income (12 months if that household has earned income) — notably longer than the 24-month elderly/disabled period several other jurisdictions in this roster use. DC's own SNAP-specific policy is not consolidated in one DCMR manual chapter; see admin_note and freshness.json for what this pack found and did not find.

This pack also found and explicitly avoided a legacy-manual-mirror trap on dcrules.elaws.us, an unofficial DCMR Title 29 mirror whose own page metadata reads 'D.C. Municipal Regulations (Last Updated: September 13, 2017)' with no HTTP error signal distinguishing it from a current page — this pack used it only to confirm DCMR chapter-numbering structure (confirming Title 29 has no dedicated SNAP-eligibility chapter comparable to Delaware's DSSM 9000) and did not rely on it for any current dollar figure or eligibility rule. dcbenefits.dhs.dc.gov, a portal URL this pack found cited by DC Hunger Solutions' own page, returned a clean HTTP 404 — a secondary-source staleness catch this pack resolved by using District Direct (districtdirect.dc.gov/ua/), confirmed live with a clean HTTP 200, as the current portal instead.
